country.name: Hungary
country.summary: Hungary sits in the Carpathian basin, far from any sea, so its vines ripen through hot continental summers and rest through hard winters. The exam wants three things above all: Tokaji, the botrytised sweet wine of the north east, with its aszú berries, puttonyos and eszencia; Egri Bikavér, the Kékfrankos led red blend called Bull's Blood; and the grapes under their Hungarian names, Furmint, Hárslevelű, Olaszrizling, Szürkebarát, Kékfrankos, Kadarka and Juhfark. The law is the European one in Hungarian dress: OEM for protected origin, OFJ for protected geographical indication. There are twenty two wine districts; the nine in this atlas are a study selection, taking in the volcanic hills of the north and west, the warm south around Villány and Szekszárd, and the sandy plain between the Danube and the Tisza.
country.overview:
The Magyars settled the Carpathian basin in 896 and brought a word for wine with them: bor is Turkic in origin, which sets Hungarian apart from almost every other wine language in Europe. Roman Pannonia had grown vines on the Balaton shore and in Sopron long before, and the medieval kingdom sent wine north to Poland, which is why the sweet wines of Tokaj carry a Polish word, szamorodni, for the unsorted bunch. The Ottoman occupation after 1526 emptied much of the south, and the Serbs who fled north from the Turks brought Kadarka to Szekszárd and Villány. Tokaj, in the Habsburg and Transylvanian borderland, flourished instead: its vineyards were ranked in classes early in the eighteenth century and a royal decree of 1737 closed the district, long before Bordeaux counted its growths.

Phylloxera arrived in the 1870s and did what it did everywhere, with one Hungarian twist: the louse cannot live in pure sand, so the plain between the Danube and the Tisza was planted on its own roots and became the country's bulk vineyard, which it remains. Four decades of state farms and co-operatives after 1949 turned the hills towards quantity for the Soviet market. The change came after 1989, and Tokaj was the first door the world walked through: foreign capital rebuilt the great estates in the early 1990s, and in the same decade local growers began making dry Furmint from single vineyards, which gave Hungary a modern white wine to set beside its historic sweet one.

The law has worn European clothes since Hungary joined the Union in 2004. OEM is the protected designation of origin, OFJ the protected geographical indication, and FN is wine without either. Beneath the labels sit twenty two wine districts, each a borvidék with its own product specification, grouped by the national body into six larger regions: Tokaj on its own; Felső-Magyarország, Upper Hungary, for Eger, Mátra and Bükk; Felső-Pannon for Sopron and the districts between it and Budapest; Balaton for the six districts around the lake, Somló among them; Pannon for Villány, Szekszárd, Pécs and Tolna; and Duna for the plain. A place name takes the suffix i to become an adjective, so Tokaji is the wine of Tokaj, Egri of Eger and Villányi of Villány.

The exam leans on Tokaj hardest, then Eger, then the grapes. Hold the aszú process and its numbers, the Bikavér blend, the Kékfrankos and Blaufränkisch equivalence, and the false friends among the white grapes, and the rest of the country falls into place behind them.
ladder: The protected designation of origin, Hungary's PDO: each of the twenty two wine districts, and some sub-districts and villages, with a product specification naming grapes, yields and ageing. Tokaj, Eger and Villány carry their own internal tiers beneath it.

The protected geographical indication, Hungary's PGI: broad zones such as Balaton, Dunántúl, Felső-Magyarország and the Duna-Tisza köze, with looser rules on grapes and yields.
Wine without a geographical indication; it may still carry a grape name and a vintage.
A wine district, twenty two in all, each governed locally by its hegyközség, the wine community, under the national council of wine communities.
Within the Tokaj PDO: dry and late harvest wines, Szamorodni (száraz or édes), Aszú at five or six puttonyos, Eszencia, Fordítás and Máslás, and the dűlő, the named single vineyard.
Classicus, Superior and Grand Superior, rising in ripeness, oak ageing and vineyard precision, applied to Egri Bikavér and Egri Csillag alike.
Classicus, Prémium and Super Prémium, the last reserved for named vineyards; Villányi Franc is the district's flagship Cabernet Franc designation.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.styles: Tokaj's great grape: searing acidity that carries the sugar of Aszú, and since the 1990s a dry white of apple, smoke and salt from single vineyards. Also grown at Somló and on the Balaton.

grapes.name: Hárslevelű
grapes.styles: Linden leaf, Furmint's partner in Tokaj: perfume, honey and body to Furmint's spine; a varietal dry or sweetish wine at Debrő near Eger and at Somló.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.styles: Welschriesling, the country's most planted white and the Balaton's workhorse: bitter almond, green apple, crisp and dry, finest at Csopak and Badacsony. It is unrelated to Riesling.

grapes.name: Kékfrankos
grapes.styles: Blaufränkisch under its Hungarian name and the most planted red: sour cherry, pepper and bright acidity, the compulsory backbone of Egri Bikavér and the signature of Sopron.

grapes.name: Kadarka
grapes.styles: The old red of the south, pale, spicy and thin skinned: a troublesome vine, prone to rot, revived at Szekszárd and on the plain, and the traditional seasoning in Bikavér.

grapes.name: Juhfark
grapes.styles: Sheep's tail, Somló's own grape: hard, smoky, high in acid and slow to open, the white that needs years.

grapes.name: Kéknyelű
grapes.styles: Blue stalk, Badacsony's rare native white, functionally female and in need of a pollinator: tight, mineral and ageworthy.

grapes.name: Szürkebarát
grapes.styles: Pinot Gris, the grey monk: fuller, honeyed whites on the Balaton's northern shore, historically off dry, and lighter aromatic versions in the Mátra.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Villány's flagship red, ripe and velvety in the warm south, graphite and plum rather than the leafy Loire style.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Flesh for the Bordeaux style blends of Villány and Szekszárd, and a permitted component in Bikavér.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: Austria's cross, soft and juicy, filling out Sopron and Eger reds and a partner in Bikavér.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: At home in the cooler north at Eger and by Lake Fertő at Sopron, light and fragrant.

grapes.name: Irsai Olivér
grapes.styles: A Hungarian cross of 1930, muscat scented and early, drunk young and cold in the Mátra and on the plain.

grapes.name: Cserszegi Fűszeres
grapes.styles: A spicy aromatic cross of Irsai Olivér and Traminer, the plain's signature cheap and cheerful white.

exam: Tokaji first: the aszú berry, the puttony, the 120 g/L floor, five and six puttonyos only, Eszencia outside the scale, Szamorodni as it comes.
Egri Bikavér: Kékfrankos compulsory, at least three varieties, Bull's Blood and the 1552 legend, and Szekszárd as the only other Bikavér.
The grape synonyms: Kékfrankos is Blaufränkisch, Olaszrizling is Welschriesling, Szürkebarát is Pinot Gris, Rizlingszilváni is Müller-Thurgau, Tramini is Gewürztraminer.
The native names: Furmint, Hárslevelű, Juhfark, Kéknyelű, Kadarka, Ezerjó, Leányka, and which district each one belongs to.
The law words: OEM, OFJ, FN, borvidék, dűlő, száraz and édes, pezsgő, and the suffix i on a place name.
The map: Tokaj in the north east, Eger and the Mátra in the north, Sopron by Lake Fertő, Badacsony and Somló on volcanic hills in the west, Villány and Szekszárd in the south, Kunság on the sand.
traps: Tokaj is the place, Tokaji the wine; Tokay in Alsace and Tocai in Friuli were different grapes and both names were retired under European law.
Puttonyos three and four are gone: a modern Aszú starts at five and carries at least 120 g/L of sugar.
Olaszrizling and Rizlingszilváni are not Riesling; the true grape is labelled Rajnai Rizling, Rhine Riesling.
Bikavér is reserved to Eger and Szekszárd; a red blend from anywhere else may not use the name.
Kékfrankos, Blaufränkisch and Lemberger are one grape in three countries, Hungary, Austria and Germany.
Somló is a single hill north west of the Balaton, not on the lake, and its grape is Juhfark, not Kéknyelű.
The plain's vines stand on their own roots because phylloxera cannot live in sand, not because Hungary escaped the louse.

cards.b: Eger (Egri Bikavér) and Szekszárd (Szekszárdi Bikavér). Both are Kékfrankos led; Szekszárd's leans on Kadarka.

questions.q: Which Hungarian grape is the same variety as Austria's Blaufränkisch?
questions.exp: Kékfrankos is Blaufränkisch, called Lemberger in Germany. Kadarka is a separate old Balkan red, Kékoportó is Portugieser, and Cabernet Franc is the flagship red of Villány in the warm south.

questions.q: Olaszrizling is the Hungarian name for which grape variety?
questions.exp: Olaszrizling, Italian Riesling, is Welschriesling and unrelated to Riesling, which Hungary calls Rajnai Rizling. Rizlingszilváni is the Hungarian name for Müller-Thurgau.

questions.q: Which two wine districts are permitted to use the name Bikavér for a red blend?
questions.exp: Bikavér, Bull's Blood, is reserved to Eger and Szekszárd, both Kékfrankos led blends of at least three varieties. Villány's flagship is Cabernet Franc and the Mátra is a white wine district.

questions.q: What does the Hungarian label term OEM denote?
questions.exp: OEM, oltalom alatt álló eredetmegjelölés, is the PDO. OFJ is the PGI and FN is wine without a geographical indication; termelői palackozás means estate bottled.

questions.q: What is the Hungarian word for a named single vineyard?
questions.exp: A dűlő is a named vineyard site, the Hungarian equivalent of a cru; Tokaj's historic classification and Eger's Grand Superior tier both rest on it.

questions.q: How many wine districts does Hungary recognise?
questions.exp: Hungary has twenty two wine districts, each a borvidék with its own product specification, grouped by the national body into six larger wine regions.

questions.q: Which Hungarian wine district lies on the shore of Lake Fertő, across the border from Austria's Burgenland?
questions.exp: Sopron sits on the Hungarian side of Lake Fertő, the Neusiedlersee, and grows Kékfrankos as Burgenland grows Blaufränkisch. Somló, Mór and Pannonhalma are inland districts of western Hungary.

questions.q: Which Hungarian label word means dry?
questions.exp: Száraz is dry, édes sweet, félédes medium sweet and pezsgő sparkling. Félszáraz, off dry, completes the sweetness ladder.

regions.name: Tokaj
regions.summary: Tokaj is Hungary's great sweet wine district and the one the exam asks hardest. It lies in the north east where the Bodrog meets the Tisza under the Zemplén hills, on volcanic rock and loess, and autumn mists off the rivers breed noble rot on Furmint and Hárslevelű. Aszú berries are picked one by one, kneaded into a paste and steeped in base wine; the finished wine must hold at least 120 g/L of sugar and spend eighteen months in oak, and is labelled five or six puttonyos. Eszencia is the free run syrup of the berries, Szamorodni the unsorted bunch. Since the 1990s the same vineyards have made dry Furmint of real class.

terroir.climate: Continental, with cold winters, warm dry summers and a long bright autumn that is the whole point. September and October bring warm days, cool nights and morning mist off the Bodrog and the Tisza, and the mist burns off by noon, so Botrytis cinerea takes hold and then dries on the berry instead of turning to grey rot. The Carpathian arc shelters the hills from the north and the Great Plain opens to the south. Rainfall is modest and the aszú harvest runs late, often into November.
terroir.soils: Volcanic through and through: rhyolite and andesite and their tuffs, weathered into nyirok, a heavy red brown clay rich in iron that holds water and gives weight and spice. Loess lies over the volcanic base on the lower slopes and caps Tokaj Hill itself, where the vineyards of Tarcal and Tokaj town give a finer, more elegant Aszú. Zeolite and clay pockets vary the picture from village to village, and the cellars are tunnels cut into the soft tuff.
terroir.topography: The Zemplén foothills run north east from Tokaj town for some forty kilometres, a chain of worn volcanic cones and ridges standing between 100 and 300 metres over the floodplain. Tokaj Hill, Kopasz-hegy, stands alone at the confluence, a single loess covered cone. Vines take the south and south west faces; the best sites sit mid slope, above the frost pocket yet within reach of the morning mist.
terroir.water: The Bodrog flows along the foot of the hills and joins the Tisza at Tokaj town. Their wide floodplain and the marshes to the south generate the autumn mists that bring botrytis, and the rivers soften the frosts of spring and autumn. Without its two rivers Tokaj would be a dry white wine district.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.styles: The spine of every Tokaji: thin skinned and botrytis prone, with acidity fierce enough to carry 150 g/L of sugar. Dry, it gives apple, pear, quince, smoke and salt, and ages for a decade.

grapes.name: Hárslevelű
grapes.styles: Linden leaf: the perfumed partner, lower in acid, bringing honey, lime blossom and body to Aszú and a softer, more aromatic dry wine on its own.

grapes.name: Sárga Muskotály
grapes.styles: Yellow Muscat, the Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains of Tokaj: a seasoning of grape and orange blossom in Aszú, and a light dry or sweet varietal.

grapes.name: Zéta
grapes.styles: A cross of Furmint and Bouvier, formerly called Oremus, early ripening and quick to take botrytis, so it goes mainly into aszú berries.

grapes.name: Kövérszőlő
grapes.styles: The fat grape, an old Transylvanian variety readmitted after years of neglect: large berries that shrivel readily, mostly for sweet wine.

grapes.name: Kabar
grapes.styles: A cross of Hárslevelű and Bouvier, a late addition to the six permitted varieties, aromatic and botrytis prone.

wines.note: Apricot, quince, orange peel, honey, saffron and botrytis smoke, cut by Furmint's acidity so the sweetness never cloys; gold, then amber with age. Serve at 10 to 12 degrees in a small pour, with foie gras, blue cheese or a fruit tart.
The free run juice of aszú berries, several hundred grams of sugar and a few degrees of alcohol: a syrup of dried apricot and honey served by the spoon, and nearly immortal.
Whole bunches pressed with their aszú berries in, so the vintage sets the sweetness: honeyed, nutty and lighter than Aszú. Good with pâté and hard cheese.
The dry version, aged under ullage: nutty, bready and saline like a fino or a vin jaune. Serve cool with soup, cured meat or aged cheese.
Green apple, quince, smoke and a saline finish, high in acid, from steel or old oak and often a single named dűlő. The modern face of Tokaj: 10 to 12 degrees, with river fish, pork or paprika dishes.
Late harvest: shrivelled and botrytised bunches pressed together without the aszú steeping and released young, fresher and lighter than Aszú. The sweet Tokaji for a by the glass list.
Traditional method sparkling wine from Furmint and Hárslevelű, bone dry and high in acid, with the smoke of the volcanic soil.

made.viticulture: Vines once stood on single stakes; today most are trained on wires in rows up the slope, and Furmint fills some two thirds of the vineyard with Hárslevelű most of the rest. The whole year aims at a late, mist fed autumn. Healthy bunches for the base wine come off in late September and October. Then the pickers return to the same rows through October and into November, taking only the shrivelled, botrytised aszú berries one by one into a small basket; a good picker gathers only a small basketful in a day. The hazards are plain: a wet autumn turns noble rot to grey rot, a dry autumn with no mist gives healthy fruit and no Aszú at all, and spring frost finds the low ground. The early eighteenth century ranking of sites still shapes where serious estates plant, and a named dűlő on a dry Furmint is now the mark of ambition.
made.winemaking: The aszú berries are kneaded into a paste, or left whole, and steeped in must, fermenting must or finished base wine of the same vintage for one to two days, so sugar, acid and botrytis flavour bleed into the liquid. The puttony was the hod of 20 to 25 kilos of berries, and the number of hods added to one gönci barrel of 136 litres gave the wine its puttonyos; since 2013 the number is a sugar band instead. The pressed wine ferments slowly in cold cellars, over weeks or months, until the yeast gives up against the sugar. It ages in oak, the gönci barrel or the larger szerednyei of about 220 litres, for at least eighteen months, in tunnels cut into the tuff at 10 to 12 degrees whose walls wear a black velvet of Cladosporium cellare, a mould that lives on alcohol vapour. The old style was long and oxidative; the modern one, since the 1990s, is topped up and bright. Eszencia drains from the heaped berries under their own weight and ferments for years to a few per cent of alcohol. Szamorodni presses whole bunches, botrytised and healthy together, dry or sweet as the year allows. Fordítás steeps fresh must or wine on paste already pressed once; Máslás ferments wine on the lees of an Aszú. Dry Furmint is pressed whole bunch, fermented in steel or neutral oak and left on its lees.

law.classification: Tokaj is one protected designation of origin, labelled Tokaj or Tokaji, covering twenty seven villages of Tokaj-Hegyalja in Hungary; a strip across the Slovak border makes wine under a separate Slovak Tokaj designation. Its vineyards were ranked in three classes early in the eighteenth century, with Mézes Mály and Szarvas at Tarcal set above the first class, and a royal decree of 1737 closed the district, among the earliest delimitations of a wine district in Europe. Six grapes are permitted: Furmint, Hárslevelű, Sárga Muskotály, Zéta, Kövérszőlő and Kabar. The sweet wines are grouped as borkülönlegesség, wine specialities, each with its own rule. The reform that took effect with the 2013 vintage abolished the three and four puttonyos categories and the old Aszú Eszencia, fixed Aszú's floor at 120 g/L of residual sugar and 9% alcohol, and set at least eighteen months in oak, so five and six puttonyos remain as optional labels for sugar bands. A dűlő name on the label means a single classified vineyard. UNESCO listed the cultural landscape, cellar rows included, in 2002.
tiers: Tokaji Eszencia
The free run juice of aszú berries, at least 450 g/L of residual sugar and only a few per cent of alcohol; it stands outside the puttonyos scale.
Tokaji Aszú 6 puttonyos
At least 150 g/L of residual sugar. The puttonyos number is a sugar band today, not a count of hods.
Tokaji Aszú 5 puttonyos
At least 120 g/L of residual sugar, the floor of the whole Aszú category since the 2013 vintage; eighteen months in oak and 9% alcohol at least.
Tokaji Szamorodni
Whole bunches pressed unsorted, botrytised and healthy berries together: száraz, dry and oxidative, or édes, sweet with at least 45 g/L.
Tokaji Fordítás and Máslás
Fordítás, a turning: must or wine steeped on aszú paste already pressed once. Máslás, a copy: wine fermented on the lees of an Aszú.
Tokaji Késői Szüretelésű
Late harvest: a sweet wine from shrivelled and botrytised fruit pressed together without the aszú steeping, briefly aged and released young.
Dry Tokaji and dűlő wines
Dry Furmint, Hárslevelű, Sárga Muskotály and blends under the same designation; a named dűlő on the label is a single classified vineyard of one village.

places.name: Tokaj-Hegyalja
places.note: The historic name of the whole district, the Zemplén foothills: a crescent of twenty seven villages from Abaújszántó in the west to Sátoraljaújhely in the north east, with Tokaj town at its southern point.

places.name: Tokaj
places.note: The town at the confluence of the Bodrog and the Tisza, beneath Tokaj Hill, Kopasz-hegy, a lone loess covered volcanic cone whose south face holds the first class Hétszőlő vineyard.

places.name: Hétszőlő
places.note: Seven vineyards: a historic first class dűlő on the loess of Tokaj Hill, long a noble holding, giving elegant, fine boned Aszú.

places.name: Tarcal
places.note: West of Tokaj Hill on the same loess, the village of the two sites ranked above the first class in the eighteenth century, Szarvas and Mézes Mály; the most refined and honeyed Aszú of the district.

places.name: Szarvas
places.note: The stag: once the Habsburg crown's own vineyard on Tokaj Hill, set above the first class and still the reference for loess grown Aszú.

places.name: Mézes Mály
places.note: The honey hollow, Szarvas's neighbour and equal in the historic ranking, a warm loess bowl a candidate should be able to place at Tarcal.

places.name: Mád
places.note: The volcanic heart of the district and the birthplace of the dry Furmint movement, ringed by first class dűlők on rhyolite tuff and red nyirok clay: Szent Tamás, Úrágya, Betsek, Király and Nyulászó.

places.name: Szent Tamás
places.note: Saint Thomas: the steep first class site above Mád that made the case for dry single vineyard Tokaji in the 2000s, smoky and saline.

places.name: Mezőzombor
places.note: At the southern edge of the volcanic hills, home to the single large Disznókő vineyard, the boar's rock, a first class site rebuilt in the 1990s.

places.name: Tállya
places.note: High in the cooler north west arm, once among the largest wine villages of Hegyalja, with a reputation for firm, slow Furmint.

places.name: Tolcsva
places.note: Chief village of the northern half, on rhyolite and clay, with first class sites such as Szentvér and Kútpatka and a princely history; the home of Oremus.

places.name: Erdőbénye
places.note: A valley village behind Tolcsva, the traditional home of the district's coopers; its vineyards sit higher and ripen later.

places.name: Bodrogkeresztúr
places.note: On the Bodrog between Tokaj and Tolcsva, with the Lapis dűlő above a long cellar row; loess and volcanic soils mixed.

places.name: Sárospatak
places.note: The Rákóczi castle town on the Bodrog near the northern end, where the princes who first made Aszú famous held court.

places.name: Sátoraljaújhely
places.note: The northern tip against the Slovak border, with the Ungvár cellar row; the vineyards over the frontier belong to the small Slovak Tokaj district.

places.name: Hercegkút
places.note: A Swabian village behind Sárospatak whose two cellar rows, Gombos-hegy and Kőporos, are part of the UNESCO listing.

producers.name: Disznókő
producers.why: The single vineyard estate at Mezőzombor rebuilt from 1992 with French capital, the clearest example of the foreign money that reopened Tokaj.

producers.name: Szepsy
producers.why: The Mád estate whose dry single vineyard Furmint turned Tokaj from a sweet wine museum into a working white wine district, and whose family name runs back to the early history of Aszú.

producers.name: The Royal Tokaji Wine Company
producers.why: Founded in 1990 at Mád by local and foreign partners, the first post communist venture in Tokaj and the house that restored single vineyard labels such as Mézes Mály.

producers.name: Tokaj Oremus
producers.why: The Tolcsva estate founded in 1993 by the house behind Vega Sicilia, a cross region exam favourite; its dry Furmint Mandolás is one of the names that rebuilt Tokaj on dry wine.

producers.name: Hétszőlő
producers.why: The historic first class vineyard on Tokaj Hill, farmed as one estate since the 1990s and a reference for elegant loess grown Aszú.

producers.name: Gróf Degenfeld
producers.why: The Tarcal estate of a historic noble family, restored after 1989 and known for a classic sweet range.

producers.name: Dobogó
producers.why: A small Tokaj town estate whose Aszú and late harvest wines show the modern, bright style at the top of the range.

producers.name: Királyudvar
producers.why: The king's court at Tarcal, an estate known for Szamorodni and dry Furmint as much as for Aszú.

producers.name: Patricius
producers.why: A Bodrogkisfalud estate with vineyards across several villages, a sound introduction to the range of Tokaji from dry to six puttonyos.

exam: The aszú process from berry to bottle: the shrivelled berry, the paste, the steeping, the slow fermentation, eighteen months in oak.
The numbers: 120 g/L for five puttonyos, 150 for six, 450 for Eszencia, 45 for sweet Szamorodni, 136 litres for the gönci barrel, 2013 for the reform.
The six grapes in order of importance, Furmint and Hárslevelű first, and what each brings.
The vocabulary: Aszú, puttonyos, Eszencia, Szamorodni száraz and édes, Fordítás, Máslás, késői szüretelésű, dűlő.
The geography: the Bodrog and the Tisza, the Zemplén hills, volcanic tuff and loess, Tokaj Hill, the villages Mád, Tarcal, Tolcsva.
The history the exam likes: the early eighteenth century classification, the 1737 decree, the 2002 UNESCO listing, the dry Furmint movement of the 1990s.
Service: 10 to 12 degrees, a small pour, foie gras, blue cheese and fruit desserts; dry Furmint with river fish and pork.
traps: Puttonyos three and four were abolished with the 2013 vintage; a modern Aszú is five or six puttonyos, or simply Aszú, and never less than 120 g/L.
Eszencia is not an Aszú grade: it is the free run juice of the berries, barely fermented, and stands outside the scale. The old Aszú Eszencia category is gone.
Szamorodni is a Polish word, not a Hungarian one, and the wine can be bone dry; do not file it as a sweet category only.
Tokaj is volcanic and loess, not limestone; the red clay is nyirok and the cellars are cut into tuff.
Tokay d'Alsace was Pinot Gris and Tocai Friulano was Sauvignonasse; neither has anything to do with Tokaj, and both names were retired under European law.
The puttonyos number no longer counts hods; it is a sugar band, and the 136 litre gönci barrel is history and arithmetic, not current law.
Hárslevelű is the partner, not the lead: Furmint is the principal grape, and Sárga Muskotály is a seasoning.

cards.f: Aszú: the modern sugar floor and the surviving puttonyos
cards.b: At least 120 g/L since the 2013 vintage. Five puttonyos is 120 g/L, six is 150 g/L; three and four are gone.

cards.f: The gönci barrel: its size and its part in the puttonyos
cards.b: 136 litres. Puttonyos once counted the hods of aszú paste, 20 to 25 kg each, steeped in one gönci barrel of base wine.

cards.f: Eszencia: what it is and its legal floor
cards.b: Free run juice of aszú berries, at least 450 g/L of sugar, a few per cent of alcohol, served by the spoon; outside the puttonyos scale.

cards.f: Szamorodni: meaning, language and two styles
cards.b: Polish for as it comes: whole unsorted bunches pressed together. Száraz is dry and oxidative; édes is sweet, 45 g/L or more.

cards.f: Tokaj's six permitted grapes
cards.b: Furmint, Hárslevelű, Sárga Muskotály, Zéta, Kövérszőlő and Kabar. Furmint leads, Hárslevelű is the partner.

cards.f: Tokaj's soils in two words, and the clay's name
cards.b: Volcanic and loess. Rhyolite and andesite tuff weather to nyirok, a red clay; loess caps Tokaj Hill at Tarcal and Tokaj.

cards.f: Two dates: the closing decree and the UNESCO listing
cards.b: A royal decree of 1737 closed the Tokaj district. The cultural landscape was listed in 2002.

cards.f: Fordítás and Máslás: the difference
cards.b: Fordítás, a turning: must or wine steeped on aszú paste already pressed once. Máslás, a copy: wine fermented on the lees of an Aszú.

cards.f: The two rivers and the hills of Tokaj
cards.b: The Bodrog joins the Tisza at Tokaj town; the Zemplén hills rise behind. The rivers' mist breeds noble rot.

cards.f: Aszú's minimum oak time and minimum alcohol
cards.b: Eighteen months in oak and at least 9% alcohol, under the rules in force since the 2013 vintage.

questions.q: Which grape is the principal variety of Tokaji Aszú?
questions.exp: Furmint fills about two thirds of Tokaj and gives Aszú its acid spine. Hárslevelű is the perfumed partner, Sárga Muskotály a seasoning, and Zéta a botrytis prone cross used mostly for aszú berries.

questions.q: Since the 2013 vintage, what is the minimum residual sugar of a Tokaji Aszú?
questions.exp: The reform set the floor at 120 g/L, the old five puttonyos level, and retired three (60 g/L) and four (90 g/L). Six puttonyos remains at 150 g/L.

questions.q: What does the word Szamorodni mean on a Tokaji label?
questions.exp: Szamorodni is Polish for as it comes: whole bunches pressed unsorted, botrytised and healthy berries together, so the wine may be dry or sweet. Aszú is the shrivelled berry and Fordítás the turning.

questions.q: What was the name of the hod in which aszú berries were traditionally measured?
questions.exp: A puttony held 20 to 25 kilos of aszú berries, and the number added to a 136 litre gönci barrel of base wine gave the puttonyos; today the number marks a sugar band.

questions.q: Which two rivers meet at the town of Tokaj?
questions.exp: The Bodrog joins the Tisza at Tokaj, and the mist off their confluence brings noble rot. The Danube meets the Tisza far to the south in Serbia, and the Hernád and Drava are elsewhere.

questions.q: Which Tokaji wine is the free run juice of aszú berries, so sweet it barely ferments?
questions.exp: Eszencia drains from the heaped aszú berries under their own weight, carries at least 450 g/L of sugar and reaches only a few per cent of alcohol; it stands outside the puttonyos scale.

questions.q: What is the minimum period a Tokaji Aszú must spend in oak?
questions.exp: The 2013 reform set eighteen months in oak as the floor, replacing the old two years in barrel and one in bottle; the cellars are tunnels cut into tuff.

questions.q: In which village do the historic vineyards Mézes Mály and Szarvas lie?
questions.exp: Both sit on the loess of Tokaj Hill at Tarcal and were ranked above the first class in the eighteenth century. Mád holds Szent Tamás and Király, Tolcsva Szentvér, and Tállya is the cool north west arm.

regions.name: Eger
regions.summary: Eger is the red wine town of northern Hungary, on the southern foothills of the Bükk, south west of Tokaj. Its name belongs to Egri Bikavér, Bull's Blood, a blend of at least three varieties on a compulsory backbone of Kékfrankos, and since 2010 to Egri Csillag, the Star of Eger, its white counterpart. The soils are rhyolite tuff, clay and loess, the cellars are cut into the tuff, and the climate is cool for Hungarian red, which keeps the wines fresh, peppery and medium bodied rather than big. Pinot Noir does well here too. The ladder is Classicus, Superior and Grand Superior, rising in ripeness, oak and precision of site.

terroir.climate: Continental and among the cooler red wine districts of Hungary. The Bükk mountains block the cold north winds, but the district lies in the north of the country at 160 to 300 metres, with real winters, a late spring and a long, bright autumn, and modest rainfall. Ripening is slower than at Villány, which is why Eger's reds lean on acidity and spice rather than weight.
terroir.soils: Rhyolite tuff is the signature: the soft, pale volcanic rock of the Bükkalja that the town's cellars are tunnelled into, weathering to light, well drained soils. Over and around it lie brown forest soils, clay and loess, and the Nagy-Eged hill above the town is limestone, which gives the most structured Bikavér. The mix gives Kékfrankos lift and the Bordeaux varieties restraint.
terroir.topography: The Bükkalja, the foothills of the Bükk, falls south from the mountains in gentle ridges and valleys around the baroque town of Eger. Vineyards take the south facing slopes from Egerszalók and Demjén in the west through Eger to Noszvaj and Ostoros in the east, with Nagy-Eged rising above the town as one of the highest vineyard hills in the country. The Debrő sub-district lies to the south west towards the Mátra.
terroir.water: The Eger stream runs through the town towards the Tisza, far away to the south east, and water plays little part in the district's climate. The thermal springs at Eger and Egerszalók belong to the spa trade, not the vineyard.

grapes.name: Kékfrankos
grapes.styles: Blaufränkisch, the compulsory base of Bikavér and a fine varietal: sour cherry, black pepper, bright acid and a firm, fresh tannin.

grapes.name: Kadarka
grapes.styles: The old spicy, pale red, difficult in the vineyard, kept in Bikavér for its perfume and bottled alone by a few estates.

grapes.name: Kékoportó
grapes.styles: Portugieser, soft and early, a filler in traditional Bikavér and in siller.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: Juicy, plummy flesh for the blend, widely planted since the state farm era.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Adds graphite and structure to Superior Bikavér; cooler and leafier here than at Villány.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Rounds the blend; a varietal from the warmer slopes in ripe years.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: A minority component of the modern blends, never the point.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Eger's cool slopes suit it: light, fragrant, red fruited Pinot Noir is the district's second reputation.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.styles: The main white, crisp and almondy, and a pillar of Egri Csillag.

grapes.name: Leányka
grapes.styles: Little girl, the soft, floral local white, often off dry; Királyleányka, the king's daughter, is its crisper relative.

grapes.name: Hárslevelű
grapes.styles: At Debrő in the south west it makes Debrői Hárslevelű, a historic honeyed, off dry white.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: A component of Csillag and a varietal from a few estates, usually unoaked.

wines.note: Bull's Blood: sour cherry, black pepper and dried herb on a Kékfrankos spine, medium bodied, fresh and spicy, with at least six months in oak. Serve at 16 to 18 degrees with goulash, paprika chicken, grilled sausage or roast duck.
The riper, longer aged tier from lower yields: darker fruit, more oak and more Bordeaux varieties in the blend, still cut by acidity. Grand Superior adds a single named vineyard.

The Star of Eger, a dry white blend of at least four varieties, half of them Carpathian basin grapes: fresh, floral, lightly aromatic and unoaked, meant to be drunk within a year or two, with river fish or a salad.
The varietal: bright, peppery and sour cherried, a cooler cousin of Burgenland Blaufränkisch, at its best from the limestone of Nagy-Eged.
Pale, fragrant and red fruited from the cool slopes, Eger's answer to the question of a Hungarian Pinot Noir.
The historic white of the Debrő sub-district: honey, linden and quince, usually off dry, a Hungarian classic from before the state farm era.
Kékfrankos rosé, pale and crisp, and the deeper siller from a longer maceration, served cold with the town's paprika cooking.

made.viticulture: Kékfrankos is a late ripener, so it takes the best south facing slopes and the warmest pockets, trained on wires and spur pruned on cordons at moderate density. The state farm years planted Zweigelt and Kékoportó for volume; the estates that rebuilt the district after 1989 pulled yields down and put Kékfrankos, Pinot Noir and the Bordeaux varieties on the better sites, and the Superior and Grand Superior tiers write lower yields into the rules. Kadarka survives in small plots because its thin skin rots in a wet September. Harvest runs from mid September for the whites through October for Kékfrankos and the Cabernets. The hazards are a northern district's hazards: spring frost in the valleys, hail off the Bükk, and the autumn rain that catches a late variety before it is ripe. The mapping of named dűlők, with Nagy-Eged the most famous, underpins the top of the ladder.
made.winemaking: Egri Bikavér is a true blend, each variety vinified on its own and assembled after fermentation. The rules ask for at least three varieties from a fixed list, Kékfrankos among them at no less than 30 per cent, and oak ageing of at least six months for Classicus and at least twelve for Superior and Grand Superior, with further bottle age before release at the upper tiers. The oak is mostly large and Hungarian, from the country's own forests, so the wood seasons rather than flavours the wine; barriques appear in Superior and in Pinot Noir. Maceration is moderate, the aim freshness and spice rather than extraction. The cellars are tunnels in the rhyolite tuff, cool and steady all year, the most famous rows in the Szépasszony-völgy on the edge of the town. Egri Csillag is the white mirror: at least four varieties, at least half of them Carpathian basin grapes such as Olaszrizling, Leányka, Királyleányka, Hárslevelű and Furmint, with the strongly aromatic grapes capped, fermented cool in steel and released young. Rosé and siller come from a short maceration of Kékfrankos.

law.classification: Eger is a protected designation of origin with its own three tier ladder, Classicus, Superior and Grand Superior, applied to Bikavér, to Csillag and to the varietal wines alike. Each step raises the minimum ripeness, cuts the yield and lengthens the oak and bottle ageing, and Grand Superior must come from a single named dűlő. The name Bikavér, Bull's Blood, is reserved by law to Eger and to Szekszárd, and the Eger rules fix the blend: at least three varieties from a list of permitted reds, Kékfrankos compulsory at a minimum of 30 per cent, no single variety allowed to turn the wine into a varietal, oak ageing of six months at the least. Egri Csillag, created in 2010, is the white blend written on the same pattern. The Debrő area in the south west, once part of the Mátra district, was moved to Eger when the districts were redrawn after 1989 and keeps its own Debrői Hárslevelű name.
tiers: Classicus
The base tier: Egri Bikavér from at least three varieties, Kékfrankos at 30 per cent or more, at least six months in oak.
Superior
Riper fruit from lower yields, at least twelve months in oak and further bottle age before release; more Bordeaux varieties in the blend.
Grand Superior
The top: a Superior from a single named dűlő, such as Nagy-Eged, with the longest ageing.
Egri Csillag
The Star of Eger, from 2010: a dry white blend of at least four varieties, at least half of them Carpathian basin grapes, no variety above half, aromatic grapes capped.
Debrői Hárslevelű
The historic off dry white of the Debrő sub-district within Eger, a protected name of its own.

places.name: Eger
places.note: The baroque town at the centre, with the castle of the 1552 siege and, on its western edge, the Szépasszony-völgy, the Valley of the Beautiful Woman, a horseshoe of cellars cut into the tuff where the town's growers pour Bikavér by the glass.

places.name: Nagy-Eged
places.note: The great Eged hill above the town, limestone rather than tuff and among the highest vineyard hills in Hungary, the source of the most structured Bikavér and Kékfrankos and the district's leading Grand Superior site.

places.name: Szépasszony-völgy
places.note: The valley of cellar rows on the town's edge, the public face of Eger wine, where a server's guests will have tasted Bikavér from the cask.

places.name: Egerszalók
places.note: West of the town below a travertine spring, a village of south facing slopes on tuff and clay that holds some of the district's best known estates.

places.name: Noszvaj
places.note: East of Eger in the Bükk foothills, higher and cooler, with cave cellars in the tuff and a reputation for fresh Kékfrankos and Pinot Noir.

places.name: Ostoros and Novaj
places.note: Two villages on the eastern slopes between Eger and the Bükk district, loess over tuff, long the source of Bikavér blending fruit.

places.name: Demjén and Andornaktálya
places.note: South west and south of the town on gentler ground, warmer sites for the Bordeaux varieties and Merlot.

places.name: Debrő
places.note: The south western sub-district at the foot of the Mátra, around Feldebrő, Aldebrő and Verpelét, moved from the Mátra district to Eger when the districts were redrawn after 1989; the home of Debrői Hárslevelű.

places.name: Verpelét
places.note: The largest village of the Debrő corner, on volcanic and loess soils, growing Hárslevelű for the historic white and Kékfrankos for the Eger blends.

places.name: Bükk
places.note: A separate wine district, east of Eger towards Miskolc on the same foothills, mostly light whites and reds; an exam will not confuse the two if a candidate remembers that Bikavér belongs to Eger.

producers.name: St. Andrea
producers.why: The Egerszalók estate whose Bikavér Superior and Grand Superior set the modern standard for the blend.

producers.name: Thummerer
producers.why: A Noszvaj family house, a long established name for Bikavér and Kékfrankos.

producers.name: Bolyki
producers.why: A winery in an old quarry above Eger, known for lively Bikavér and for the varietal Kékfrankos of the district.

producers.name: Gróf Buttler
producers.why: Named for a historic count, with vineyards on Nagy-Eged and a reputation built on Grand Superior Bikavér from that hill.

producers.name: Juhász Testvérek
producers.why: A larger estate of the Eger district making a full range from Csillag to Superior Bikavér, a safe reference for the style at every tier.

exam: Egri Bikavér: at least three varieties, Kékfrankos compulsory at a minimum of 30 per cent, oak for at least six months, and the name reserved to Eger and Szekszárd.
The legend: the 1552 siege of Eger castle and the Turks who thought the defenders drank bull's blood.
Egri Csillag, the Star of Eger, the white blend of 2010, at least four varieties and half Carpathian basin grapes.
The ladder: Classicus, Superior, Grand Superior, and what rises at each step.
The geography: the Bükk, the Bükkalja, rhyolite tuff, the Szépasszony-völgy cellars, Nagy-Eged, and Debrő with its Hárslevelű.
Kékfrankos is Blaufränkisch; Kékoportó is Portugieser; Leányka is Fetească Albă; the exam will ask the synonyms here as much as anywhere.
traps: Bikavér is a blend, never a single grape: the question that asks which grape is Bull's Blood wants the answer that it is a Kékfrankos led blend.
Eger sits under the Bükk, not the Mátra; the Mátra is the next district west and makes mostly white wine.
Szekszárd also makes a Bikavér, with more Kadarka, so Eger is not the only Bull's Blood.
Debrői Hárslevelű is a white and off dry, though it comes from the Eger district; do not file it under Tokaj.
Egri Csillag is the white blend; Csillag means star, and the wine is not a sparkling wine.
The old Bull's Blood of the export years was a bulk red; the modern blend is tiered and regulated, and Classicus is its floor, not its summit.

questions.q: Which grape variety is compulsory in an Egri Bikavér blend?
questions.exp: Kékfrankos must make up at least 30 per cent of the blend. Kadarka, Zweigelt and Cabernet Franc are on the permitted list but none is required.

questions.q: What is the minimum share of Kékfrankos required in an Egri Bikavér?
questions.exp: The Eger rules set a floor of 30 per cent for Kékfrankos in every tier of Bikavér, with ceilings that stop any one variety from turning the blend into a varietal.

questions.q: What does the name Bikavér mean in English?
questions.exp: Bika is bull and vér is blood. The legend ties the name to the 1552 siege of Eger, when the Turks took the red wine on the defenders' beards for bull's blood.

questions.q: Which white wine of Eger is a regulated blend created in 2010?
questions.exp: Egri Csillag, the Star of Eger, was created in 2010 as the white counterpart of Bikavér: at least four varieties, half of them Carpathian basin grapes. The others are varietal or historic names.

questions.q: Which is the base tier of the Eger classification?
questions.exp: Eger's ladder runs Classicus, Superior, Grand Superior, the last from a single named dűlő. Prémium belongs to Villány's ladder, not Eger's.

questions.q: What is the minimum period in oak for a Classicus Egri Bikavér?
questions.exp: Classicus, the base tier of Egri Bikavér, must spend at least six months in oak; Superior and Grand Superior ask at least twelve months and further bottle age before release.

questions.q: Which mountain range shelters the Eger district from the north?
questions.exp: Eger lies on the Bükkalja, the southern foothills of the Bükk. The Mátra is the district to the west, the Zemplén rises over Tokaj, and the Bakony stands north of Lake Balaton.

questions.q: Into which rock are the cellars of Eger's Szépasszony-völgy cut?
questions.exp: The Bükkalja is rhyolite tuff, a soft volcanic rock easily tunnelled and steady in temperature. Basalt belongs to Badacsony and Somló, Leitha limestone to Sopron's lakeside, and sand to the plain.

regions.name: Mátra
regions.summary: The Mátra is the white wine district on the southern foothills of the Mátra mountains, west of Eger and north east of Budapest, around the town of Gyöngyös. It is one of Hungary's largest districts by area and was long called Mátraalja. The vines stand on loess and brown forest soil over volcanic andesite, sheltered by the mountains, and give crisp, aromatic whites: Olaszrizling, Rizlingszilváni, Szürkebarát, Ottonel Muskotály, Irsai Olivér, Tramini, Chardonnay and Sauvignon Blanc, with Kékfrankos and Zweigelt the reds. The exam wants its synonyms and its place on the map more than any single wine.

terroir.climate: Continental, with the Mátra range standing as a wall against the north wind, so the south facing foothills are warmer and drier than their latitude suggests; summers are hot, winters cold, and the autumn long and sunny. Rainfall is moderate and spring frost is the main risk on the lower, flatter ground towards the plain.
terroir.soils: Volcanic andesite and its tuffs form the base of the Mátra, the same volcanic belt that built the Zemplén further east, but the vineyards sit mostly on what lies over them: loess, brown forest soil and clay on the slopes, with sandier ground towards the plain. The volcanic bedrock lends a faint smokiness to the better Olaszrizling and Szürkebarát.
terroir.topography: The southern foothills of the Mátra, the range that holds Kékes, the highest point in Hungary at just over a thousand metres, fall in broad ridges to the Great Plain. The vineyards lie between 150 and 350 metres from Gyöngyöspata in the west through Gyöngyös and Nagyréde to Abasár and Markaz in the east, above the town of Gyöngyös.
terroir.water: No river or lake shapes the district; small streams run south off the mountains to the Zagyva and the Tarna, and so to the Tisza. Shelter and aspect, not water, make the climate.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.styles: Welschriesling, the backbone white: green apple, bitter almond, crisp and dry, the everyday wine of Gyöngyös.

grapes.name: Rizlingszilváni
grapes.styles: Müller-Thurgau under its Hungarian name, soft, floral and early, for simple fresh whites.

grapes.name: Szürkebarát
grapes.styles: Pinot Gris, lighter and more aromatic here than on the Balaton, a pear and honey dry white.

grapes.name: Ottonel Muskotály
grapes.styles: Muscat Ottonel, grapey and rose scented, dry or off dry, the district's aromatic calling card.

grapes.name: Irsai Olivér
grapes.styles: The muscat scented Hungarian cross of 1930, picked early for a light, fragrant white drunk cold and young.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Tramini on a Hungarian label: lychee and rose, usually off dry.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Fresh, unoaked or lightly oaked, a staple of the larger wineries.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grassy and crisp from the cooler higher sites, a recent success.

grapes.name: Kékfrankos
grapes.styles: The main red, light and peppery, more often rosé or siller than a serious red.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: Soft, juicy reds and rosés for early drinking.

grapes.name: Kadarka
grapes.styles: A survivor in old plots, pale and spicy, rarely bottled alone.

wines.note: Dry, light to medium bodied, green apple and almond with a faint smoke from the volcanic base; the carafe white of northern Hungary, served cold with fish soup, chicken paprikash or a cheese plate.
Pinot Gris in a fresh, dry key: pear, white flowers and a soft texture, lighter than the Badacsony version. Pork, poultry, mild cheeses.
Muscat Ottonel, rose petal and grape, dry or just off dry, low in acid: an aperitif wine, or the match for a fruit salad or a mild curry.
Light, intensely aromatic and low in alcohol, the spring wine of Hungary, drunk within a year of the harvest, very cold, on its own or with salads.
Kékfrankos or Zweigelt rosé, pale, strawberry scented and dry, the summer wine of the district's cellars.
A light, peppery red from the warmer slopes, lower in tannin than Sopron's, for charcuterie and grilled meat.

made.viticulture: The Mátra was a volume district under the state farms and co-operatives, and the vineyards still show it: long rows on wires at moderate density, machine harvesting on the flatter ground, and large holdings in the hands of a few big wineries beside many small growers. The varieties were chosen for reliability and aroma, which is why Rizlingszilváni, Irsai Olivér and Ottonel Muskotály, all early and generous, sit beside Olaszrizling. The better estates have moved up the slope, cut yields and planted Szürkebarát, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay on the cooler, higher sites below the forest line. Harvest begins in late August for the earliest aromatic grapes and runs through September; the main hazards are spring frost on the lower ground, hail off the mountains, and rot in a wet autumn on the thin skinned Muscats. Ripeness comes easily; freshness is the thing a grower works for.
made.winemaking: The district's method is the modern aromatic white method: early picking for acidity, gentle pressing, cold settling, cool fermentation in stainless steel with selected yeasts, early bottling and no malolactic conversion, so the wines keep their primary fruit and are sold within a year. Oak is rare and used only for Chardonnay, Szürkebarát or a Kékfrankos from the better estates, in large neutral casks or older barriques. Off dry styles, with a little residual sugar left in Muscat, Tramini and Szürkebarát, are traditional and still sell. Rosé and siller are made by a short maceration of Kékfrankos or Zweigelt, and the few serious reds are fermented in open vats and aged briefly in oak. The large wineries also make tank method sparkling wine from the same aromatic base. The style is clean, light and fragrant, and the exam will not ask more of it than that.

law.classification: Mátra is one of the twenty two wine districts, a protected designation of origin whose product specification lists the permitted varieties, mostly white, and the yields; wines that fall outside it go out under the broader Felső-Magyarország geographical indication, which the Mátra shares with Eger and Bükk. The district was long called Mátraalja, the foot of the Mátra; when the districts were redrawn after 1989 the name was shortened and the Debrő corner on its eastern edge was moved to Eger. There is no internal ladder of the Eger or Villány kind; the label carries the district name, the grape and the sweetness, and the rare single vineyard wine names its dűlő.

places.name: Gyöngyös
places.note: The market town at the centre of the district and the seat of its largest wineries, at the foot of the road that climbs to Kékes; Gyöngyös Olaszrizling is the everyday white of the region.

places.name: Gyöngyöstarján
places.note: West of Gyöngyös on loess over andesite, a village of family estates and one of the district's better addresses for Olaszrizling and Szürkebarát.

places.name: Nagyréde
places.note: South west of Gyöngyös, the home of the district's great co-operative winery of the state era, long one of the country's large exporters of fresh aromatic white wine.

places.name: Gyöngyöspata
places.note: The western end of the district, with old vineyards on the lower slopes; Muscat and Irsai Olivér country.

places.name: Abasár and Markaz

places.name: Kékes
places.note: Hungary's highest peak, just over a thousand metres, which shelters the district; the vines stop far below it at the forest line.

producers.name: Nagyrédei Szőlők
producers.why: The Nagyréde winery, the successor to the state era co-operative, a large exporter and the source of much of the Mátra wine a server will meet abroad.

producers.name: Dubicz
producers.why: A Gyöngyös family estate of the modern generation, known for Olaszrizling, Szürkebarát and Sauvignon Blanc from the higher slopes.

producers.name: Benedek Pince

producers.name: Centurio
producers.why: A Gyöngyöspata estate at the western end, a good reference for the district's aromatic whites and Kékfrankos.

exam: Place it: the southern foothills of the Mátra, around Gyöngyös, west of Eger, north east of Budapest, and under Kékes, Hungary's highest peak.
Know it as a white wine district of aromatic, crisp, early drinking wines, one of the largest in Hungary by area.
The synonyms are the examinable core: Szürkebarát is Pinot Gris, Rizlingszilváni is Müller-Thurgau, Tramini is Gewürztraminer, Olaszrizling is Welschriesling, Ottonel Muskotály is Muscat Ottonel.
The old name Mátraalja and the move of Debrő to Eger when the districts were redrawn.
Soils in one line: loess and brown forest soil over volcanic andesite.
traps: The Mátra is a white district; Bikavér belongs to Eger next door, not here.
Mátra and Mátraalja are one district under two names, the second the older.
Szürkebarát is Pinot Gris, not Pinot Blanc, and not a monk's wine in any other sense than its name.
Rizlingszilváni and Olaszrizling are both false friends of Riesling; the true grape is Rajnai Rizling.
Kékes is the peak, not a village or a grape; Kéknyelű is the Badacsony grape and Kékfrankos the red.

cards.b: Southern foothills of the Mátra mountains around Gyöngyös, west of Eger; a white wine district of crisp, aromatic, early drinking wines.

cards.b: Pinot Gris, Müller-Thurgau, Gewürztraminer.

cards.b: Olaszrizling is Welschriesling, unrelated to Riesling. Ottonel Muskotály is Muscat Ottonel, the district's aromatic signature.

cards.b: Mátraalja, the foot of the Mátra. The Debrő corner, with its Hárslevelű, moved to the Eger district when the districts were redrawn after 1989.

cards.f: Mátra soils in one line
cards.b: Loess and brown forest soil over volcanic andesite; the mountain shelters the south facing foothills.

cards.f: Kékes: what and how high
cards.b: Hungary's highest peak, in the Mátra range, just over a thousand metres; the vines stop far below it.

cards.f: Irsai Olivér: what kind of wine
cards.b: A muscat scented Hungarian cross of 1930: light, very aromatic, low in alcohol, drunk young and cold.

questions.q: Szürkebarát, a grape of the Mátra, is the Hungarian name for which variety?
questions.exp: Szürkebarát means grey monk and is Pinot Gris; it makes a light dry white in the Mátra and a fuller one on the Balaton. Pinot Blanc, Chardonnay and Sylvaner are separate varieties.

questions.q: Rizlingszilváni, widely planted in the Mátra, is which grape?
questions.exp: Rizlingszilváni is Müller-Thurgau, the old Riesling and Sylvaner cross. Welschriesling is Olaszrizling, and true Riesling is Rajnai Rizling in Hungary.

questions.q: Which town is the centre of the Mátra wine district?
questions.exp: Gyöngyös sits at the foot of the Mátra range and holds the district's largest wineries. Eger is the neighbouring district to the east, Miskolc the city of the Bükk, Kecskemét the market town of the Kunság plain.

questions.q: What was the Mátra wine district called before its name was shortened?
questions.exp: Mátraalja means the foot of the Mátra. The shortening came in the same reorganisation that moved the Debrő corner from the Mátra to Eger.

questions.q: Which colour of wine makes up most of the Mátra's production?
questions.exp: The Mátra is a white wine district built on Olaszrizling, Szürkebarát, Rizlingszilváni and the Muscats; Kékfrankos and Zweigelt are a minority, often as rosé.

questions.q: To which of Hungary's six larger wine regions does the Mátra district belong?
questions.exp: Felső-Magyarország, Upper Hungary, groups the Mátra with Eger and Bükk, the three districts of the northern hills; Sopron belongs to Felső-Pannon and Badacsony to the Balaton region.

questions.q: Which Hungarian cross, planted in the Mátra for a light aromatic white, dates from 1930?
questions.exp: Irsai Olivér was bred in 1930 and is drunk young and cold for its muscat scent. Cserszegi Fűszeres is a later cross from Irsai Olivér, Zenit a Hungarian white cross, and Zéta a Tokaj cross of Furmint and Bouvier.

regions.name: Sopron
regions.summary: Sopron is Hungary's far western red wine district, a historic town between the last hills of the Alps and the shallow steppe lake the Hungarians call Fertő and the Austrians Neusiedlersee, with Burgenland on the far shore. It is the capital of Kékfrankos: the same grape Austria grows as Blaufränkisch across the water, here peppery, bright and medium bodied in one of the coolest and rainiest climates in the country. Zweigelt, Pinot Noir and the Bordeaux varieties follow, with crisp Zöld Veltelini and Chardonnay among the whites. The soils are gneiss and mica schist in the hills, loess and Leitha limestone towards the lake. The exam wants the lake, the grape and its synonym, and the border.

terroir.climate: Cool, wet and windy by Hungarian standards: the district sits at the eastern foot of the Alps, open to Atlantic weather from the west, with rainfall among the highest of any Hungarian wine district and summers that stay moderate. Lake Fertő, shallow and wide, softens the frosts, holds warmth into the autumn and keeps the air moving, which dries the bunches. Kékfrankos ripens late and keeps its acidity here, which is the whole character of the wine.
terroir.soils: Two worlds. The Sopron Hills to the west are the easternmost spur of the Alps, crystalline gneiss and mica schist with brown forest soils, giving taut, mineral reds. Towards the lake the ground changes to loess, clay and the Leitha limestone that the Romans quarried at Fertőrákos, which gives rounder, more generous Kékfrankos. Gravel and sand appear on the lake shore.
terroir.topography: The town lies in a basin between the wooded Sopron Hills, which rise to about 550 metres on the Austrian border, and the flat western shore of Lake Fertő. Vineyards face east and south east off the hills and spread across the low rises around Balf and Fertőrákos towards the reed beds. Kőszeg, a historic town fifty kilometres south on the same border, is an outlying part of the district under the Kőszeg Hills.
terroir.water: Lake Fertő is the district's weather maker: Central Europe's largest steppe lake, barely a metre deep, ringed with reeds, warming fast in summer and tempering the autumn nights. Its cultural landscape, shared with Austria, was listed by UNESCO in 2001. The Ikva stream runs through the town to the lake.

grapes.name: Kékfrankos
grapes.styles: Blaufränkisch: Sopron's signature, sour cherry, blackberry, black pepper and bright acidity, medium bodied, from fresh and juicy to serious and age worthy from the schist and limestone sites.

grapes.name: Zweigelt
grapes.styles: The Austrian cross of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent, soft and plummy, a blending partner and an easy varietal.

grapes.name: Pinot Noir
grapes.styles: Suited to the cool lakeside climate, light, fragrant and increasingly serious.

grapes.name: Merlot
grapes.styles: Flesh and softness for the cuvées, ripening well on the warmer limestone slopes.

grapes.name: Cabernet Sauvignon
grapes.styles: Firm and leafy in this climate, used in small shares of the blends.

grapes.name: Cabernet Franc
grapes.styles: Cooler and more peppery than at Villány, a component of the better red blends.

grapes.name: Syrah / Shiraz
grapes.styles: A recent arrival on the warmest sites, peppery and lean.

grapes.name: Grüner Veltliner
grapes.styles: Zöld Veltelini, the Austrian white over the border, crisp and peppery here too.

grapes.name: Chardonnay
grapes.styles: Fresh and mineral from the schist, sometimes oaked.

grapes.name: Sauvignon Blanc
grapes.styles: Grassy and bright in the cool climate, a growing plot.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer
grapes.styles: Tramini, aromatic and off dry, the old aromatic white of the Poncichter cellars.

grapes.name: Leányka
grapes.styles: The soft local white, floral and gentle, from older plantings.

wines.note: Sour cherry, blackberry and cracked black pepper, bright acidity, moderate tannin and a cool, savoury finish; from fresh and unoaked to structured and aged in large oak. Serve at 16 degrees with roast goose, paprika stews, sausage or duck.
Kékfrankos with Zweigelt, Merlot or the Cabernets, rounder and darker than the varietal, a bistro red for grilled meats.
Light, red fruited and fragrant from the lakeside climate, among Hungary's better Pinot Noirs; chicken, salmon, mushroom dishes.
Grüner Veltliner on the Hungarian shore: white pepper, green apple and a crisp finish, a match for the district's lake fish and a schnitzel.
Kékfrankos rosé, pale, crisp and red berried, served cold through the summer.
Mineral and fresh from the schist soils, oaked or unoaked, a white for cream sauces and poultry.

made.viticulture: Sopron is a late ripening, high acid district and its growers work for ripeness rather than freshness. Kékfrankos is a vigorous vine with big bunches and thin skins, so it is trained on wires, spur pruned, leaf thinned on the lake side and cropped to moderate yields to concentrate it; the best growers green harvest and pick late, into mid or late October, and some farm organically or biodynamically on the exposed, windy slopes where the lake air keeps fungal pressure down. The schist and gneiss sites in the hills ripen later and give smaller, tighter berries; the loess and limestone sites towards the lake ripen earlier and fuller. The hazards are a cool, wet summer that leaves Kékfrankos green and thin, late spring frost on the flat lakeside rows, and the rain that a westerly brings in September. The German speaking growers of old, the Poncichter, planted beans between the rows and lived on both crops; a few of their terraced plots and cellars survive in the town.
made.winemaking: The modern Sopron red is made to keep its pepper and acid: destemmed or part whole berry, fermented in open vats or steel with moderate extraction and a short to medium maceration, then aged in large Hungarian or Austrian oak of several hundred litres, or in older barriques, for a year or more at the top of the range. New oak is used sparingly, since Kékfrankos takes on wood easily and loses its fruit. Entry level Kékfrankos is bottled young in steel for its juice. Pinot Noir follows a Burgundian pattern in barrique, and the cuvées are assembled after separate fermentation. Whites are pressed whole bunch and fermented cool in steel, with Chardonnay sometimes fermented in cask. Rosé and siller come from a short maceration of Kékfrankos. The oldest cellars of the town are the Poncichter houses with their vaulted ground floors; the newer estates have built on the slopes above the lake.

law.classification: Sopron is one of the twenty two wine districts, a protected designation of origin whose product specification names the permitted varieties and yields, with Kékfrankos at its head, and which covers both the town's own vineyards and the outlying Kőszeg area to the south. In the national grouping it belongs to Felső-Pannon, Upper Pannon, with Neszmély, Etyek-Buda, Mór and Pannonhalma, the districts that run from the Austrian border towards Budapest. There is no internal ladder of the Eger or Villány type: a label carries the district name, the grape, the sweetness and, from the better estates, a named dűlő or a village such as Balf or Fertőrákos. The Fertő and Neusiedlersee cultural landscape, shared with Austria, has been a UNESCO site since 2001.

places.name: Sopron
places.note: The old town itself, Roman Scarbantia, a walled medieval and baroque centre that voted in 1921 to stay in Hungary rather than join Austria; the Poncichter cellars line its outer streets and the vineyards climb the hills behind it.

places.name: Lake Fertő
places.note: The Neusiedlersee: a shallow, reedy steppe lake shared with Austria, the district's weather maker and a UNESCO cultural landscape since 2001, with Burgenland's Blaufränkisch villages on the far shore.

places.name: Balf
places.note: A spa village on the lake shore south east of the town, on loess and limestone, the home of several of the district's leading estates and the source of its roundest Kékfrankos.

places.name: Fertőrákos
places.note: The lakeside village of the Roman limestone quarry, Leitha limestone that still shows in the stone of Vienna, with vineyards on the rise between the quarry and the reeds.

places.name: The Sopron Hills
places.note: The easternmost spur of the Alps, gneiss and mica schist rising to about 550 metres on the Austrian border, whose east facing lower slopes give the district's tautest, most mineral Kékfrankos.

places.name: Kőszeg
places.note: A historic walled town fifty kilometres south of Sopron on the Austrian border, the district's outlying part under the Kőszeg Hills, cooler still, with Kékfrankos and crisp whites.

producers.name: Weninger
producers.why: The Balf estate of a family that also farms across the border in Burgenland, the reference for serious single vineyard Kékfrankos on both sides of the lake.

producers.name: Pfneiszl
producers.why: A family estate on the hills above Sopron whose Kékfrankos and cuvées show the schist side of the district.

producers.name: Taschner
producers.why: A Sopron family house, a sound introduction to the district's Kékfrankos, Zweigelt and Zöld Veltelini.

producers.name: Luka
producers.why: A small Sopron estate known for fresh Kékfrankos and Pinot Noir from the lakeside slopes.

producers.name: Ráspi
producers.why: The Fertőrákos estate on the lake shore, a maker of concentrated reds and sweet wines in a district better known for lightness.

exam: Place it: far western Hungary, the town of Sopron, between the Alps' last hills and Lake Fertő, the Neusiedlersee, with Austria's Burgenland across the water.
The grape: Kékfrankos, which is Blaufränkisch, cool, peppery and bright; Sopron is called its capital.
The soils: gneiss and mica schist in the hills, loess and Leitha limestone by the lake.
The history: Roman Scarbantia, the Poncichter bean growers, the 1921 vote to stay Hungarian, the UNESCO lake of 2001.
The grouping: Felső-Pannon, with Neszmély, Etyek-Buda, Mór and Pannonhalma.
traps: Sopron is in Hungary and Burgenland in Austria, though they share a lake, a grape and a history; a Soproni Kékfrankos is not an Austrian wine.
Lake Fertő and the Neusiedlersee are one lake under two names.
Kékfrankos is Blaufränkisch and Lemberger, not Kadarka and not Zweigelt, which is its cross with St. Laurent.
Sopron is a red district in a mostly white country; its whites are secondary.
Kőszeg belongs to the Sopron district though it lies fifty kilometres to the south.
Sopron is among Hungary's coolest and wettest districts, not its warmest; that is Villány in the south.

cards.f: Sopron: where, and across which lake from which Austrian region
cards.b: Far western Hungary at the foot of the Alps, on Lake Fertő, the Neusiedlersee; Burgenland lies on the far shore.

cards.f: Sopron's signature grape and its two other names
cards.b: Kékfrankos: Blaufränkisch in Austria, Lemberger in Germany. Sopron is called the Kékfrankos capital.

cards.f: Sopron's soils: hills and lakeside
cards.b: Gneiss and mica schist in the Sopron Hills, the Alps' last spur; loess, clay and Leitha limestone towards the lake.

cards.f: The Poncichter of Sopron
cards.b: German speaking vintners who planted beans between the vines, from Bohnenzüchter, bean grower; their cellars line the old town.

cards.f: Two dates for Sopron: the vote and the lake
cards.b: 1921, the plebiscite that kept Sopron in Hungary. 2001, the UNESCO listing of the Fertő and Neusiedlersee landscape.

cards.f: Sopron's climate in one line
cards.b: Cool, wet and windy, the Alps' edge open to Atlantic weather, the shallow lake softening frost and holding autumn warmth.

cards.f: Sopron's wine region grouping and its companions
cards.b: Felső-Pannon, Upper Pannon, with Neszmély, Etyek-Buda, Mór and Pannonhalma.

cards.f: Zweigelt: the parentage
cards.b: An Austrian cross of 1922, Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent; soft, plummy, a partner to Kékfrankos at Sopron.

questions.q: Which grape variety is the signature of the Sopron wine district?
questions.exp: Sopron is called the capital of Kékfrankos, the grape Austria grows as Blaufränkisch across Lake Fertő. Zweigelt and Pinot Noir are secondary here and Kadarka belongs to the south.

questions.q: By which name is Lake Fertő known in Austria?
questions.exp: Fertő and Neusiedlersee are one shallow steppe lake shared by Hungary and Austria, with Sopron on the Hungarian shore and Burgenland on the other. The other three are Alpine lakes in Carinthia.

questions.q: Zöld Veltelini, a white grape of Sopron, is the Hungarian name for which variety?
questions.exp: Zöld is green and Veltelini is Veltliner: the grape Austria grows as Grüner Veltliner across the lake, crisp and white peppered on the Hungarian shore too. Roter Veltliner is a different grape.

questions.q: Which country lies directly across the border from the Sopron wine district?
questions.exp: Sopron sits against the Austrian border, with Burgenland across the lake and over the hills; Slovakia lies to the north, Slovenia and Croatia to the south.

questions.q: Which rocks make up the Sopron Hills behind the town?
questions.exp: The Sopron Hills are the easternmost spur of the Alps, crystalline gneiss and mica schist. Basalt belongs to Badacsony and Somló, loess and sand to the plain, limestone and red sandstone to Csopak on the Balaton; Leitha limestone lies only by the lake at Fertőrákos.

questions.q: Which historic walled town fifty kilometres south of Sopron is an outlying part of the Sopron wine district?
questions.exp: Kőszeg, under the Kőszeg Hills on the Austrian border, belongs to the Sopron district though it lies fifty kilometres south. Szombathely, Mosonmagyaróvár and Győr are towns of western Hungary outside the district.

questions.q: To which of Hungary's larger wine regions does the Sopron district belong?
questions.exp: Felső-Pannon, Upper Pannon, groups Sopron with Neszmély, Etyek-Buda, Mór and Pannonhalma. Felső-Magyarország is Eger, Mátra and Bükk; Pannon is Villány, Szekszárd, Pécs and Tolna.

questions.q: Zweigelt, Sopron's second red grape, is a cross of which two varieties?
questions.exp: Zweigelt was bred in Austria in 1922 from Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent, which is why it sits so naturally beside Kékfrankos on both shores of the lake.

regions.name: Badacsony (Balaton)
regions.summary: Badacsony is a flat topped basalt hill on the northern shore of Lake Balaton, the largest lake in Central Europe, and the name of the white wine district around it. Basalt and basalt tuff cap Pannonian sand and clay, the lake throws light and warmth back onto the south facing slopes, and the wines are fuller and rounder than Hungary's other volcanic whites: Olaszrizling for everyday, Szürkebarát as the historic rich style, Rajnai Rizling and Furmint for structure, and Kéknyelű, the rare native blue stalk, as the district's own treasure. Badacsony is one of six districts in the Balaton region, with Csopak's Olaszrizling to the east and the south shore's Balatonboglár across the water.

terroir.climate: Continental with a sub-Mediterranean softness that is the lake's gift: the water, warm and shallow, reflects sunlight onto the slopes, holds heat into a long, mild autumn and keeps frost off the hillsides, while the humidity it breathes out favours full ripeness and, in some years, noble rot. Summers are hot and the growing season long; the north facing slopes behind the hill are forest.
terroir.soils: A basalt cap and its tuff on the summit and upper slopes, weathering to dark, iron rich, stony clay that gives the wines their weight, smoke and salt; beneath it the Pannonian sandstone, sand and clay of the old inland sea, with patches of loess, on the gentler lower slopes where the lighter wines grow. The same pattern repeats on every witness hill of the basin.
terroir.topography: Badacsony rises to 437 metres, a little over 300 above the lake, a flat topped butte with columns of basalt, the organ pipes, on its upper flanks. It is one of a family of witness hills in the Tapolca basin, the stumps of ancient volcanoes whose basalt caps protected the soft Pannonian beds beneath: Szent György-hegy, Csobánc, Gulács, Tóti-hegy and the castle hill of Szigliget. Vines take the south and south west faces from the shore road to the foot of the basalt.
terroir.water: Lake Balaton: 77 kilometres long, a few metres deep, the Hungarian sea, warming fast in summer and cooling slowly, a mirror for the sun and a buffer against frost. Its evaporation keeps the air humid, and its six districts, Badacsony, Balatonfüred-Csopak, Balaton-felvidék, Balatonboglár, Zala and Nagy-Somló, make up the Balaton wine region.

grapes.name: Olaszrizling
grapes.styles: Welschriesling, the most planted grape of the whole lake: green apple, bitter almond and a crisp, dry, saline finish, fuller on Badacsony's basalt and finest at Csopak.

grapes.name: Szürkebarát
grapes.styles: Pinot Gris, the historic Badacsony wine: rich, honeyed and full, off dry or sweet in the old days, now mostly dry, with pear and smoke from the basalt.

grapes.name: Kéknyelű
grapes.styles: Blue stalk, the rare native white, functionally female and needing a pollinator such as Budai Zöld: lean, mineral, high in acid and slow to open, the district's own grape and its proudest.

grapes.name: Riesling
grapes.styles: Rajnai Rizling, Rhine Riesling, the true grape: taut, citrus and stone fruit, mineral from the basalt, a speciality of a few estates.

grapes.name: Furmint
grapes.styles: Tokaj's grape in its western home, firmer and smokier here, dry and structured.

grapes.name: Budai Zöld
grapes.styles: Green of Buda, an old variety kept largely to pollinate Kéknyelű, bottled alone by a few growers as a light dry white.

grapes.name: Rózsakő
grapes.styles: Rose stone, a cross of Kéknyelű and Budai Zöld named for the stone on Badacsony hill, aromatic and easier to grow than its parent.

grapes.name: Gewürztraminer

wines.note: Dry, medium bodied, green apple and almond with the smoke and salt of basalt; the wine of the lakeside fish fry, served cold with fogas, the Balaton pike perch, or fried carp.
Pinot Gris full and honeyed, pear, quince and a smoky finish, dry in the modern style and off dry in the old one; the historic name of the hill. Roast pork, goose liver, mushroom dishes.
Pale, lean and mineral, lime, green herb and wet stone, with acidity that needs a few years to soften; the collector's white of the Balaton. Serve at 10 to 12 degrees with freshwater fish or poultry.
True Riesling from the basalt, dry and taut, citrus and stone fruit with a petrol note in age.
The lake's other great address for the grape, east along the shore: finer and more saline than Badacsony's, from limestone and red sandstone under a growers' charter of its own.
Szürkebarát or Olaszrizling picked late, sometimes botrytised in the lake's humidity: honeyed, moderately sweet, a historic style of the hill, with fruit desserts or on its own.
Traditional and tank method sparkling wine from the south shore, Chardonnay and Olaszrizling based, crisp and clean, one of Hungary's main sources of sparkling wine.

made.viticulture: Vines on Badacsony run in rows across and up the slope between stone walls and old press houses, many of them on terraces cut into the basalt scree; the upper sites on stony clay are hand worked and the lower ones on sand are easier and often machine harvested. Olaszrizling is the reliable vine, moderate in vigour and late enough to keep acid in the lake's warmth. Kéknyelű is the difficult one: its flowers are functionally female, so it sets fruit only with a pollinator planted among it, traditionally Budai Zöld, and its yields are low and uneven, which is why it nearly vanished in the state era and why its revival since the 1990s is the district's pride. Harvest runs from mid September for the aromatic grapes into October for Szürkebarát and Kéknyelű, and late into autumn for the sweet styles. Hazards are rot in a humid, wet September, hail, and in the old days over cropping for the sweetish Szürkebarát of the co-operatives. Organic farming has taken hold on the witness hills.
made.winemaking: The district makes white wine in two registers. The fresh register is modern: whole bunch pressing, cold settling, cool fermentation in stainless steel, a few months on fine lees and early bottling, dry, for Olaszrizling and the aromatic grapes. The traditional register is fuller: fermentation and ageing in large old oak casks of the Balaton cellars, longer lees contact and sometimes malolactic conversion, for Szürkebarát, Kéknyelű, Furmint and Rajnai Rizling, which gives the smoky, broad, saline wines that basalt is known for. Residual sugar was the hill's habit in the twentieth century, when Badacsonyi Szürkebarát meant an off dry, almost sweet wine; the leading estates have gone dry, and the sweet wines are now late harvest and botrytis bottlings made on purpose. Kéknyelű is handled gently in old wood and released a year or two after the harvest, since its acidity needs time. On the south shore the larger wineries make sparkling wine by both the tank and the traditional method, and rosé from Kékfrankos is made by short maceration all around the lake.

law.classification: Badacsony is one of the twenty two wine districts, a protected designation of origin covering the hill and the witness hills of the Tapolca basin along the northern shore, with a product specification that lists the permitted varieties and yields; the broader Balaton geographical indication catches the wines outside it. In the national grouping it belongs to the Balaton wine region, which has six districts: Badacsony, Balatonfüred-Csopak, Balaton-felvidék, Balatonboglár on the south shore, Zala in the west and Nagy-Somló on its own hill to the north west. There is no internal ladder in law; the better estates name their hill, Szent György-hegy or Csobánc, or their dűlő, and Csopak's growers hold their Olaszrizling to a charter of their own that goes beyond the district rules.
